summary:
We developed a Search Engine for Space-Base Analog Sites + Mission Design + Ecological Impact + Simulations. What if the environments we need to understand other worlds are already here on Earth?
Today we have access to valuable scientific information about planetary geology, extreme environmental conditions and the organisms that inhabit our own world, however, connecting these datasets to identify important relationships and support future space exploration is still a challenge. That’s why we created BioSpace. We uses open planetary and Earth data to find and characterize terrestrial analogues of the Moon and Mars. Through a weighted comparison of geospatial variables, our platform ranks locations based on their similarities and lets users adjust the analysis to different mission goals. But we wanted to go further. BioSpace also explores local wildlife, environmental and mission risks, human habitability and wellbeing, resource needs, and estimated fungal survival under different conditions on both Mars and Earth.  Our analysis combines normalized data, weighted criteria, mathematical algorithms and customizable mission profiles, taking into account factors such as destination, crew size and mission duration. All of this comes together in an interactive 3D experience that makes scientific data and hypotheses easier to explore and understand. With BioSpace, we use Earth to understand other worlds while learning how to better protect our own.
details:
What it does

BioSpace is a search engine for space analogs. It finds the places on Earth that best match a planned Moon or Mars mission, explains why, and lets you walk them in 3D before you go.

A guided assistant asks six questions:

  • who you are
  • what you want to test
  • where the real mission goes (Shackleton, Malapert, Nobile or the Mare Tranquillitatis pit on the Moon; Arcadia Planitia, Deuteronilus Mensae, Melas Chasma or Elysium Mons on Mars)
  • crew size and duration
  • the conditions you need
  • the emergency you want to rehearse

BioSpace then ranks 22 Earth analog sites and returns the top three, each with two scores:

  • Fidelity: how closely the site resembles the target for that goal, based on similarity of the terrain features, geology, subsurface, isolation and site type.
  • Feasibility: how realistic it is to run the campaign there, based on logistics, crew capacity, safety, access and data confidence.

Users can edit the weights, make conditions mandatory and see which sites were discarded and why. A sensitivity test reruns the ranking 40 times with random changes to the weights (±20%) and the balance (±0.1). It shows whether the top three holds.

Each site has a full profile in a command center:

  • map
  • side-by-side comparison
  • climate chart and risk traffic light system
  • month-by-month accessibility calendar with sources for each month
  • in-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU)
  • flora, fauna, and extremophiles
  • laboratories for astrobiology, extremophile research, mycology, and mission design
  • minerals and soil composition
  • volcanic activity
  • humidity and temperature
  • potential habitable footprints at each site
  • glossary

Finally, a 3D simulator lets users walk or drive a rover at a target site and its Earth analog, with each world’s gravity. One key switches between the two worlds at the same spot. The same jump rises about 3.1 m on the Moon, 1.35 m on Mars and 0.49 m on Earth. Users can run a field protocol, an emergency drill and a cargo landing, also in a Meta Quest headset.

Benefits and intended impact

Choosing an analog site today means piecing together fact sheets, papers and field reports, and the decision is hard to defend. BioSpace turns that into a transparent, repeatable choice. A research team can justify a site to its funders with the method, weights, sensitivity results, discarded sites and sources in one downloadable report.

The same tool also serves:

  • teachers, who get an interactive class on why we train on Earth
  • research Centers and Space Companies
  • museums and geoparks, which can connect their own landscape to another world

Our goal is to make analog site selection open, explainable and accessible beyond the few experts who do it today.

How we built it

  • App: HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript. Everything runs in the browser, using Google Cloud Computer as infraestructura.
  • 3D landing: Three.js nad Babylon.js.
  • Simulator: Babylon.js with WebXR, for virtual reality on Meta Quest 2. We tested it with the IWER WebXR emulator.
  • Maps: Leaflet for the 2D map, plus a 3D globe.
  • Site catalog: JSON, prepared with geospatial analysis in Python.
  • Data: open NASA data, such as the NSSDC planetary fact sheets, plus sources for each site. Every source is listed with its link inside the app.
  • Testing: 61 built-in self-tests and automated browser tests with Playwright.
  • Language: full Spanish and English interface with a one-click switch.

What makes it creative

  • Two scores instead of one. Every site gets a fidelity score and a feasibility score. You see the trade-off between the most faithful site and the most feasible one instead of a single number that hides it.
    • a five-test field protocol: test jump, soil sample, science station, rover traverse, and a CAPCOM link with real signal delay;
    • an emergency drill with an alarm and a timer;
    • a cargo landing with a plume exclusion zone;
    • a simulated crew and suit telemetry.
    • Guided demos for three user profiles (a lunar campaign planner, a teacher and a research center testing water extraction) walk through the whole tool in a few minutes, with autoplay.
    • The interface switches between English and Spanish with one click.
    • It works with a keyboard and a screen reader, and has a high-contrast mode.
    • Generates a PDF file for the whole assesement

What our team considered

  • Honesty about data: every value is labeled as verified, sourced or estimated, and draft sites are marked as drafts. Scores are our own model, not official NASA ratings.
  • Safety and access: the access calendar flags seasonal closures and current travel advisories.
  • Accessibility: high-contrast mode, keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels and two languages.
  • Low cost: it runs on any laptop and uses an affordable VR headset.
  • Sustainability: a free plan for everyone, plus paid Expert and Enterprise plans for teams that need to justify their choice.
